questions.question: How does Encapsulation (information hiding) impact software testing in Object-Oriented systems?

options.A: Internal state is hidden within private fields, making it harder to inspect state after test execution and verify postconditions without dedicated accessor methods or state observers.
options.B: Encapsulation prevents classes from being compiled.
options.C: Encapsulation makes all methods static.
options.D: Encapsulation eliminates all software bugs automatically.

questions.explanation: Because private instance variables cannot be accessed directly by external test cases, observing whether state was correctly mutated (observability) requires getters, inspecting return values, or state instrumentation.

questions.question: What testing challenge is introduced by Inheritance in Object-Oriented programming?

options.A: Inherited methods operate in a new subclass context with potentially overridden state or collaborator methods, meaning inherited methods cannot simply be assumed correct without re-testing.
options.B: Inherited methods cannot be executed.
options.C: Subclasses cannot have constructors.
options.D: Base classes must be deleted after inheritance.

questions.explanation: Even if method m() passed all tests in superclass Base, when inherited by SubClass, it may interact with overridden methods or new subclass invariants, necessitating context-sensitive retesting.

questions.question: What testing challenge arises from Polymorphism and Dynamic Binding?

options.A: A single method call site (e.g. obj.draw()) can bind dynamically to many different subclass implementations at runtime, requiring tests to cover all feasible concrete receiver types.
options.B: Polymorphism causes memory leaks in all compilers.
options.C: Polymorphism requires writing code in C.
options.D: Polymorphism eliminates the need for test oracles.

questions.explanation: Dynamic dispatch means the actual code executed is decided at runtime based on the object's dynamic type, creating a combinatorial explosion of polymorphic call targets that must be tested.

questions.question: Why can Abstract Classes and Interfaces NOT be tested directly as units?

options.A: Because they cannot be directly instantiated without providing concrete implementations for their abstract method declarations.
options.B: Because they have no names.
options.C: Because Java bans testing abstract classes.
options.D: Because they only contain integer constants.

questions.explanation: Abstract classes and interfaces contain unimplemented method signatures and cannot be instantiated with 'new'. Testing their contracts requires concrete subclasses, test doubles, or mock objects.

questions.question: What is 'State-based Testing' of an Object-Oriented class?

options.A: Testing that sequences of method invocations correctly transition an object between valid internal states according to its Class State Machine.
options.B: Testing software across different US states.
options.C: Testing only the main method.
options.D: Testing while the computer is turned off.

questions.explanation: An object encapsulates mutable state. State-based testing treats methods as state transitions, executing sequences of calls to verify that transitions, guards, and invariants are preserved.

questions.question: What is a 'State Definition Anomaly' in class testing?

options.A: When an instance variable is left uninitialized or corrupted by a method call sequence, placing the object into an inconsistent internal state.
options.B: When a class has too many comments.
options.C: When a method has more than 3 parameters.
options.D: When an interface is implemented twice.

questions.explanation: A state definition anomaly occurs when method operations violate class invariants or fail to properly initialize/update interrelated instance variables.

questions.question: In class testing, what is a 'Class Invariant'?

options.A: A condition that must hold true for every valid instance of the class at all stable points (after constructor execution and after every public method call).
options.B: A constant that cannot be printed.
options.C: A method that takes no arguments.
options.D: The class filename on disk.

questions.explanation: A class invariant (e.g. balance >= 0, or size <= capacity) expresses fundamental structural truth about the object's valid state that must be maintained across all public operations.

questions.question: What is the 'flattened class' testing approach for inheritance?

options.A: Treating a subclass as if all inherited methods were copied directly into it, and testing the entire flattened set of methods in the subclass context.
options.B: Deleting all subclasses.
options.C: Compressing the class bytecode.
options.D: Converting object-oriented code into procedural C.

questions.explanation: Class flattening conceptually expands the subclass to include all inherited methods as if locally defined, ensuring thorough test coverage of inherited operations in the subclass environment.

questions.question: What is 'Method Interleaving' testing in class state testing?

options.A: Executing arbitrary permutations and sequences of different public methods (e.g. push, pop, top, push, clear) to discover sequence-dependent defects.
options.B: Writing methods in two languages simultaneously.
options.C: Running two compilers at once.
options.D: Deleting private methods.

questions.explanation: Method interleaving tests whether methods behave correctly when executed in diverse sequences, catching bugs caused by unexpected state remnants from prior calls.

questions.question: How does the 'Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)' relate to testing derived classes?

options.A: If SubClass is an LSP-compliant subtype of BaseClass, any test case written for BaseClass should pass when executed with a SubClass instance without altering correctness.
options.B: Subclasses must have fewer methods than base classes.
options.C: Subclasses cannot throw exceptions.
options.D: Subclasses must be static.

questions.explanation: LSP states that objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without affecting program correctness. Re-executing base class tests on subclasses validates LSP conformance.

questions.question: What is an 'equivalent state' in class state-machine testing?

options.A: Two distinct internal state representations that produce identical observable behavior for all subsequent method call sequences.
options.B: Two states with the same integer ID.
options.C: States in two different programs.
options.D: States with the same number of variables.

questions.explanation: In behavioral testing, two states are equivalent if no sequence of operations can distinguish between them based on observable outputs and return values.

questions.question: What is a 'Sneaking Method' anomaly in OO testing?

options.A: A method that inadvertently modifies instance state that it should have treated as read-only, violating encapsulation or contracts.
options.B: A method that runs in background threads.
options.C: A method with no name.
options.D: A method that is never called.

questions.explanation: A sneaking method introduces unintended state changes (unwanted side-effects) on variables that are outside its defined functional responsibility.

questions.question: In OO unit testing (such as with JUnit or NUnit), what is the role of the '@BeforeEach' / 'setUp()' fixture method?

options.A: To create a fresh, clean instance of the object under test before each individual test case, ensuring test isolation.
options.B: To compile the test code.
options.C: To print debugging logs to console.
options.D: To delete old test files.

questions.explanation: Test isolation is critical in OO testing: setUp() reconstructs a pristine object state before every test method executes, preventing test order leakage and shared state contamination.

questions.question: What is a 'Mock Object' in OO testing?

options.A: A simulated collaborator object that verifies expected method invocations, parameter values, and return interactions with the class under test.
options.B: A cartoon drawn by developers.
options.C: An object that throws an error on every line.
options.D: A database backup file.

questions.explanation: Mocks are test doubles programmed with expectations (which methods should be called, with what arguments) that verify behavioral interactions between components in isolation.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Stub and a Mock in object testing?

options.A: A stub provides pre-canned answers to calls made during the test; a mock verifies that specific method calls and interaction protocols actually occurred.
options.B: Stubs are written in Java; mocks are written in C++.
options.C: Stubs test databases; mocks test web pages.
options.D: There is no difference.

questions.explanation: Stubs provide canned state/data to the system under test (state verification), while Mocks verify behavioral interactions and call protocols (behavior verification).

questions.question: What problem does Dependency Injection (DI) solve from a testing perspective?

options.A: It decouples classes from hardcoded dependencies, allowing testers to easily inject mock or stub objects for unit testing.
options.B: It accelerates CPU clock rates.
options.C: It eliminates the need for constructors.
options.D: It replaces relational databases.

questions.explanation: When classes instantiate concrete dependencies directly with 'new', swapping them with test doubles is difficult. Dependency injection allows test frameworks to supply test doubles seamlessly.

questions.question: Why is testing generic / parameterized classes (e.g. 'Stack<T>') challenging?

options.A: Because the class must behave correctly for diverse type parameters (primitive wrappers, custom objects, comparable types, nullable types).
options.B: Because generic classes cannot be compiled.
options.C: Because generics are deleted at compile time in all languages.
options.D: Because generic types cannot be instantiated.

questions.explanation: Generic components must be verified against heterogeneous type arguments, including types with custom equals/hashCode, edge-case comparison behaviors, and null semantics.

questions.question: What is 'Object Mutation Testing'?

options.A: Applying mutation operators specifically tailored to OO language features, such as changing access modifiers, swapping super/this calls, and modifying overriding relationships.
options.B: Mutating DNA in biology.
options.C: Deleting object constructors.
options.D: Running code on different operating systems.

questions.explanation: Class-level mutation operators mutate OO constructs: access modifiers (public -> private), super calls, method overrides, and polymorphic references.

questions.question: What is an 'illegal state transition' in class testing?

options.A: Calling a method when the object is in a state that does not permit it (e.g. calling pop() on an EmptyStack), which should trigger a defined exception.
options.B: Moving a computer across state lines.
options.C: Calling a private method.
options.D: Running a test twice.

questions.explanation: State machines define valid transitions. Invocations in invalid states (like pop() on empty stack) must be verified to fail gracefully with expected exceptions (e.g. UnderflowException).

questions.question: What is 'Round-Trip Path Testing' on an object's state transition diagram?

options.A: Testing sequences of method calls that transition an object out of a state and eventually bring it back to that exact same state.
options.B: Testing tests in reverse order.
options.C: Testing round-off errors in floating-point math.
options.D: Testing network pings.

questions.explanation: Round-trip testing verifies reversible operations (e.g. insert followed by delete, open followed by close), checking that returning to the original state leaves no residual corruptions.
